changelog: Replace Example E1 with labeled example en_us_1591 to teach the model to avoid cutting inside names/titles and to prefer keeping multiword name/title units intact (addresses the 'splitting multiword units' finding).

Replace Example E2 with labeled example en_us_1102 to demonstrate the danger of cuts that leave existential or predicate fragments (e.g. 'may be the presence ...') so such high-contra positions rank very low (addresses the 'preverbal/existential fragments' finding).

Replace Example E3 with labeled example en_us_1192 to illustrate cohesion loss when cuts split quantifier/numeral frames and lists, guiding the ordering away from such cuts (addresses the 'quantifier/list splitting' finding).
findings: The prompt underestimates how destructive a following predicate/qualification can be: cuts that leave a preverbal fragment, an incomplete predicate, or an existential/qualification (e.g. 'may be the presence ...') are often contradicted or made misleading by what follows and must be ranked far lower.

The prompt downplays cohesion loss from splitting multiword units: breaking titles/names, a noun/verb head from its essential modifiers or objects, list items or quantifier frames frequently destroys translatability and should be penalised strongly.

diagnosis.why: Replacing the three examples accidentally encouraged earlier, within-unit cuts (especially inside multiword names/titles and before predicates) while removing a clear anti-list-splitting signal; that made many short-span (≤3–10 word) cut positions look better but harmed long-span cohesion and increased harmful splits of lists/predicate frames in larger bins.
diagnosis.lesson: A subsequent revision should preserve training signals that discourage cutting inside multiword names/titles and splitting coordinated/quantifier frames, and avoid examples that implicitly demonstrate or reward preverbal/predicate isolation.
